newsitem.title: USA: President Kennedy aide McGeorge Bundy dead at 77.
newsitem.headline: President Kennedy aide McGeorge Bundy dead at 77.

text.p: McGeorge Bundy, a top aide to Presidents John F. Kennedy and Lyndon Johnson and an architect of U.S. policy in Vietnam, died on Monday of a heart attack. He was 77.
Bundy died at Massachusetts General Hospital, where he was admitted on Saturday, according to a hospital spokeswoman.

A Republican who supported President Eisenhower in 1952 and 1956, Bundy was appointed Special Assistant on National Security by his Democratic successor Kennedy in 1961. He continued in that position under Johnson until 1966.

President Bill Clinton called Bundy "a central figure in the postwar history of our nation." He said Bundy had served Kennedy and Johnson through difficult times, including the Cuban missile crisis and the early days of the Vietnam war.

Along with Defence Secretary Robert McNamara and Secretary of State Dean Rusk, Bundy was instrumental in formulating a policy that saw the United States commit more and more troops and resources to South Vietnam.
Bundy was born on March 30, 1919, into a prominent New England family where talk of politics and issues was daily fare. His father Harvey Bundy himself had held several top government positions.

He graduated first in his class from Yale in 1940 and joined the Army, contributing to the strategic invasion plans to take Sicily and France. After the war, he went to Washington to work for the agency helping rebuild Europe, until he left to join Thomas Dewey's presidential campaign.
Bundy became a professor at Harvard and rose to the second-ranking position in the university before leaving the Republican Party to work for Kennedy's election.

Kennedy offered him the National Security position, where Bundy was a key player in determining what issues came to the president's attention, including Vietnam. He stayed on after Kennedy's assassination and became a crucial foreign policy consultant for Johnson.
As the fighting spread and U.S. choices dwindled, Bundy opposed a negotiated withdrawal from Vietnam and became a leading spokesman for Johnson's stance on continuing the war.
He resigned in 1965, but did not disassociate himself from the administration's policies.
Bundy was thought by many to embody the academic intelligencia associated with the Kennedy Administration.
"Bundy is one of the keenest intellects I ever encountered," said Robert McNamara in his book "In Retrospect: The Tragedy and Lessons of Vietnam."

"Kennedy always wanted to bring together the world of power and the world of ideas, and he turned more systematically than any other president to the universities. Bundy suited his theories and his needs perfectly," Kennedy adviser Arthur Schlesinger Jr. said When Bundy left the White House.

Clinton praised Bundy for his long stewardship of the Ford Foundation and said his books and articles "brought a compelling intelligence to some of the most important issues of our times -- foremost among them, reducing the danger of nuclear weapons."

Bundy was president of the Ford Foundation from 1966 through 1979, leaving to teach at New York University, where he was professor emeritus since 1989. Since 1990 he chaired the Committee on Reducing Nuclear Danger at the Carnegie Corp., where he was scholar in residence since 1993.
He is survived by his wife Mary and four sons, Stephen, Andrew, William and James. His survivors also include two brothers and two sisters.
